questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.

questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

Excluding participants solely because their outcome data are missing can be an appropriate modified ITT analysis for D2; assess the missing outcomes in D3. An eligible participant with an observed outcome omitted from the assignment analysis, or analysed in the wrong randomized group, is a distinct D2 concern. Record whether exclusions occurred before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded, but timing alone does not establish availability or the exclusion reason. An observed value omitted from analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. An analyzed count below the randomized count alone does not establish inappropriate analysis; if the exclusion mechanism cannot support a reasonable probable judgment, retain no_information. When 2.6 is no, probably_no, or no_information, assess 2.7 conditionally: could the wrong-group analysis or exclusions substantially affect this Result if the assignment-analysis failure occurred? Keep uncertainty about the analysis mechanism explicit. Assess potential impact using the participants affected, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance; demonstrated actual bias or a sensitivity analysis is not required, and no precise percentage rule applies.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.
questions.official_guidance: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

questions.bias_construct: Whether failure to analyse participants in their randomized group could substantially affect the result.
considerations: Carry the inappropriate or uncertain analysis mechanism from 2.6 into this conditional impact judgment. Explain how the affected participants or observations could change this selected estimate, considering their outcomes, prognostic differences and the analysis assumptions. A small component of a restriction does not settle the impact of other components.

Treatment stopping, unmeasured outcomes and measured values omitted by an analysis rule are different facts. Stopping alone establishes neither omission nor bias; a censoring rule alone does not establish how many measured values were omitted. Preserve uncertainty about actual availability and selection, including possible outcome-dependent loss.

A source-supported probable judgment is valid without a numerical bound, demonstrated bias or a sensitivity analysis. Explain why the restriction is plausibly important or negligible for this endpoint; a small or balanced count alone is insufficient. Low potential impact does not make an inappropriate analysis appropriate.
questions.decision_rule: Assess whether the number analysed in the wrong group or excluded was sufficient for substantial impact. There is no precise percentage rule: fewer than 5% may still matter for rare outcomes or exclusions strongly related to prognostic factors.
evidence_needed: Counts and reasons for participants analysed in the wrong group or excluded, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance of exclusions.
invalid_shortcuts: a group label without exclusion counts

was between 99.4 and 108.8%, the intra- and interday coefficients of variation were 1.8 to 12.6% and 0
to 2.7%, respectively, and the range of detection of the method was 0.025 to 15.1 mg/liter. Finally, for
pyrazinamide, accuracy was between 100.0 and 102.1%, intra- and interday coefficients of variation were
1.8 to 4.0% and 0.0 to 2.0%, respectively, and the range of detection of the method was 0.2 to 60.1
mg/liter.
Subsequently, a noncompartmental analysis with WinNonLin (version 6.3) software (Pharsight Corp.,
Mountain View, CA, USA) was performed to compute the values of the pharmacokinetic parameters for
rifampin, as described previously (11).
Safety and tolerability. Physical examination, testing of vital signs (including systolic and diastolic
blood pressure and heart rate), assessment of weight, biochemistry testing (AST, ALT, -glutamyl
transpeptidase, alkaline phosphatase, and creatinine), and hematology testing (hemoglobin, hematocrit,
red cell count, platelet count, total white cell count with differential) took place at screening and after
1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 weeks of treatment. In addition, at these visits the safety history was assessed
and concomitant medication was registered. Determination of fasting blood glucose levels was per-
formed only at screening.
Investigators reviewed each adverse event and assessed its relationship to drug treatment as
unrelated, possibly related, or related according to predefined definitions.
The severity of adverse events, including laboratory abnormalities, was classified following the U.S.
National Institutes of Health Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE; version 4.0) (25)
and reviewed by a data safety monitoring board.
Microbiological assessments. Spot sputum samples were collected for Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) staining
and direct microscopy before enrollment. For confirmation of the diagnosis, isolates from screening
cultures were identified as members of the M. tuberculosis complex using an AccuProbe assay (Gen-
Probe, San Diego, CA, USA) or a BD MGIT TBc identification test (BD Diagnostics, Sparks, MD, USA). These
screening isolates were also tested for susceptibility to streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol
by a commercial broth macrodilution test for the mycobacterial growth indicator tube (MGIT) platform
(SIRE; BD Bioscience, Erembodegem, Belgium) or a GenoType MTBDRplus assay (Hain Lifescience GmbH,
Nehren, Germany).
Pooled overnight (16 h) sputum samples were collected at the baseline and at days 2, 4, 7, 14, 21,
28, 35, 42, 49, and 56. All samples were processed for culture in the MGIT automated liquid culture
system as well as for culture on solid Lowenstein-Jensen medium (LJ); the latter was incubated for 8
weeks at 37°C. Pooled overnight sputum samples were also processed for counting of the colonies in
serial sputum samples; samples were diluted and plated in quadruplicate on selective Middlebrook 7H11
plates. The numbers of CFU per milliliter of sputum were calculated after a minimum of 21 days of
incubation at 37°C. In addition, the time to positivity (TTP) of the MGIT liquid culture was determined for
these samples to assess the change in TTP over time.
The study endpoints were defined as the time to culture conversion on LJ and in MGIT and the
proportion of patients that achieved culture conversion after 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 weeks, in addition to the
change in TTP in MGIT and the number of log CFU on Middlebrook 7H11 plates over time.
All sputum samples for microbiology were processed in the research microbiological laboratory of
KCMC. Procedures were performed according to the REMoxTB laboratory and quality manuals (26).
Statistical analysis. On the basis of experience obtained during a pharmacokinetic study of anti-TB
drugs in Botswana (27), it was estimated that 20 patients per arm would be needed to detect an increase
in total rifampin exposure in plasma of at least 35%, defined from the area under the concentration-
versus-time curve up to 24 h after the dose (AUC0-24), after an increase in the rifampin dose from 600
to 900 mg and from 900 to 1,200 mg (one-sided type I error, 0.05; 80% power; between-arm t test). To
obtain a more thorough insight into the safety and tolerability of higher than standard doses of rifampin,
the total number of patients per study arm was targeted at 50.
Pharmacokinetic parameters were presented descriptively and were log transformed before further
statistical analysis. Between-group differences in pharmacokinetic parameters were tested by one-way
analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test for the time to the maximum plasma concentra-
tion (Tmax). Univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed for each of the arms
separately to assess the effects of gender, age, and body weight on the AUC0-24 and the maximum
plasma concentration (Cmax) of rifampin.
Safety was expressed as the incidence of adverse events by severity and relatedness, according to the
CTCAE criteria (25). The number of patients experiencing each event classified by system organ class
(SOC) was further specified for grade 3 adverse events.
The time to culture conversion between arms was compared using Cox proportional hazards
regression and by plotting Kaplan-Meier survival estimates. Cox proportional hazards regression was also
used to evaluate the effect of the actual rifampin dose received (in milligrams per kilogram) and the
rifampin exposures achieved (AUC0-24 and Cmax). The effect of exposure was evaluated by dichotomizing
each continuous parameter and by entering total and peak exposures as continuous variables. The
AUC0-24 or Cmax values of rifampin, isoniazid, or pyrazinamide were compared between those with and
those without grade 3 to 5 adverse events using an independent-groups t test.

22|ABSTRACT
23|In a multiple-dose-ranging trial, we previously evaluated higher doses
24|of rifampin in patients for 2 weeks. The objectives of the current study were to ad-
25|minister higher doses of rifampin for a longer period to compare the pharmacoki-
26|netics, safety/tolerability, and bacteriological activity of such regimens. In a double-
27|blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, phase II clinical trial, 150 Tanzanian patients
28|with tuberculosis (TB) were randomized to receive either 600 mg (approximately 10
29|mg/kg of body weight), 900 mg, or 1,200 mg rifampin combined with standard
30|doses of isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol administered daily for 2 months.
31|Intensive pharmacokinetic sampling occurred in 63 patients after 6 weeks of treat-
32|ment, and safety/tolerability was assessed. The bacteriological response was as-
33|sessed by culture conversion in liquid and solid media. Geometric mean total expo-
34|sures (area under the concentration-versus-time curve up to 24 h after the dose)
35|were 24.6, 50.8, and 76.1 mg · h/liter in the 600-mg, 900-mg, and 1,200-mg groups,
36|respectively, reflecting a nonlinear increase in exposure with the dose (P 0.001).
37|Grade 3 adverse events occurred in only 2 patients in the 600-mg arm, 4 patients in
38|the 900-mg arm, and 5 patients in the 1,200-mg arm. No significant differences in
39|the bacteriological response were observed. Higher daily doses of rifampin (900 and
40|1,200 mg) resulted in a more than proportional increase in rifampin exposure in
41|plasma and were safe and well tolerated when combined with other first-line anti-TB
42|drugs for 2 months, but they did not result in improved bacteriological responses in
43|patients with pulmonary TB. These findings have warranted evaluation of even
44|higher doses of rifampin in follow-up trials. (This study has been registered at Clini-
45|calTrials.gov under identifier NCT00760149.)

2|here is an urgent need to improve the treatment of tuberculosis (TB), considering
3|that approximately 10.4 million people develop active TB and 1.8 million people die
4|from it each year (1). Since its introduction in the 1960s, rifampin has been considered
5|the cornerstone in TB treatment (2). It is active against Mycobacterium tuberculosis in
6|the exponential growth phase, and it possesses activity against nonreplicating persis-
7|tent bacilli. It is applied in a daily dose of 10 mg/kg of body weight, which corresponds
8|to 600 mg in most populations. The evidence underpinning the selection of this
9|recommended dose of rifampin is scant and based on the idea that effective rifampin
10|plasma concentrations were achieved with this dose. This was coupled with a fear of
11|adverse effects at higher doses and cost considerations for programmatic implemen-
12|tation at the time that rifampin was introduced (in the 1960s and 1970s) (3).
13|Accumulating evidence suggests that higher doses of rifampin may be more
14|effective and, thus, could lead to shortening of the duration of TB treatment. More
15|specifically, in vitro experiments in a pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model of TB
16|showed that higher levels of exposure to rifampin kill the mycobacteria more rapidly
17|and prevent the emergence of resistance to this drug (4). Experiments in mice have also
18|shown that the current 10-mg/kg dose of rifampin is at the lower end of the dose-
19|response curve and that an increase in the dose leads to enhanced sterilizing activity
20|and a decrease in the duration of treatment for pulmonary TB in mice (5-8). A
21|systematic review identified 14 randomized controlled clinical trials that evaluated
22|doses of rifampin of up to 1,200 mg (20 mg/kg) administered at different dosing
23|intervals for the treatment of pulmonary TB (9). Most of the trials were performed
24|before 1980, and only four of them were considered to be of high quality according to
25|published guidelines, yet several of them suggested an advantage in terms of the
26|likelihood of culture conversion among patients receiving at least 900 mg of rifampin
27|(9, 10). These combined findings and the results of more recent clinical studies on the
28|concept of high-dose rifampin (11, 12) encouraged us to develop a series of clinical
29|trials to thoroughly investigate higher doses of rifampin for pulmonary TB. We have
30|previously reported on our initial multiple-dose-ranging trial in which we evaluated
31|higher doses of rifampin in patients with pulmonary TB for a short period of 2 weeks
32|(the Pan African Consortium for the Evaluation of Antituberculosis Antibiotics
33|[PanACEA] HIGHRIF study 1) (13). Here we report on the findings of our second trial
34|(PanACEA HIGHRIF study 2; ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00760149), which was initi-
35|ated at the same time as the PanACEA HIGHRIF study 1. In PanACEA HIGHRIF study 2,
36|we evaluated higher doses of rifampin for a longer period of 2 months.
37|The objectives of this clinical trial were to determine the effect of a higher than
38|standard dose of rifampin (900 and 1,200 mg of rifampin compared to 600 mg) on the
39|pharmacokinetics of rifampin, on the occurrence of adverse events, and on the bacte-
40|riological response of M. tuberculosis when these higher doses of rifampin were
41|combined with other first-line anti-TB drugs for 2 months.
42|RESULTS
43|Patients. A total of 150 smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis patients, predomi-
44|nantly male patients (n 135, 90%), were randomized. The patient characteristics were
45|found to be similar across the three arms of the study (Table 1).
46|Pharmacokinetics. Pharmacokinetic data were available for 23, 21, and 19
47|patients in the 600-, 900-, and 1,200-mg dose groups, respectively. The majority of
48|patients in these groups (91%, 91%, and 90%, respectively) were male; the median
49|ages were 35, 36, and 31 years, respectively, and the median weights were 57, 54,
50|and 56 kg, respectively, similar to the median values for the patients in the whole
51|group.

55|more than dose-proportional increase in the level of exposure with the dose (Table 2;
56|Fig. 1). More than dose-proportional increases in the average maximum plasma con-

9|MAMS-TB-01).
10|MATERIALS AND METHODS
11|Research sites and ethics. This study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00760149) was conducted
12|at the Kilimanjaro Clinical Research Institute (KCRI), Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre (KCMC), and
13|affiliated study sites (Kibong'oto National Tuberculosis Hospital and Mawenzi Regional Hospital, Kiliman-
14|jaro region, Tanzania) and at the Ifakara Health Institute (IHI)/Bagamoyo Research and Training Centre
15|(BRTC) and affiliated study sites (Bagamoyo and Dar es Salam, Tanzania).
16|Approval for this study was obtained from the Kilimanjaro Christian Medical College Research Ethics
17|and Review Committee (CRERC), the Ifakara Health Institute Institutional Review Board (IHI-IRB), and the
18|Tanzanian National Health Research Ethics Subcommittee (NatHREC).
19|Patients. Patients were included in the trial if they were between the ages of 18 and 65 years, had
20|newly diagnosed pulmonary TB (confirmed by a positive smear of at least two spontaneously produced
21|specimens using Ziehl-Neelsen [ZN] staining), and provided informed consent. Female patients agreed
22|to take measures to prevent pregnancy during the initial phase of treatment. Exclusion criteria included
23|treatment with anti-TB drugs in the past 3 years; a body weight of less than 50 kg; ALT or AST levels 3
24|times the upper limit of normal; clinical liver disease (presenting with nausea, jaundice, and tender
25|hepatomegaly); a serum creatinine level higher than the upper limit of normal; a relevant history or
26|current condition that might interfere with drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion; the
27|use of antiretroviral treatment or the expectation of the use of antiretroviral treatment within 2 months;
28|a Karnofsky score of 40; pregnancy or breast-feeding; and rifampin-resistant or multidrug-resistant
29|(MDR) TB.
30|Study design. The study was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, phase II clinical trial.
31|After stratification for gender and HIV status, eligible patients were randomized to 600 mg, 900 mg, or
32|1,200 mg rifampin as an oral daily dose during the 2-month intensive phase.
33|Randomization occurred in blocks of 6 patients containing 2 subjects in each arm. A randomization
34|list was created using the ASELECT formula in Microsoft Excel 2007 software. In accordance with the
35|guidelines of the Tanzanian National TB Program, additional treatment of TB during the intensive phase
36|further consisted of isoniazid (300 mg), pyrazinamide (1,600 mg), and ethambutol (1,100 mg) once daily
37|for 2 months.
38|Dependent on the study site, subjects were hospitalized for the intensive phase of treatment or were
39|treated at home. During hospitalization, medication intake was directly observed by study staff. If the
40|subjects were not hospitalized, treatment adherence was verified by home-based or facility-based
41|directly observed therapy (DOT), meaning that patients were instructed to take their medication after
42|breakfast in the presence of a counselor or a nurse. Furthermore, administration of study drug was
43|documented with dispensing and drug accountability forms.
44|Drug treatment. TB treatment during the intensive phase was administered as fixed-dose combi-
45|nation (FDC) tablets containing rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (the tablets contained
46|these four drugs at 150, 75, 400, and 275 mg, respectively) manufactured by Sandoz, Mumbai, India, and
47|donated to the Tanzanian TB program by Novartis through the WHO Global Drug Facility, which monitors
48|the quality of anti-TB drugs according to WHO standards. The study medication consisted of four of these
49|FDC tablets together with either two capsules of placebo (600-mg arm), one capsule with 300 mg
50|rifampin (Rifadin; Sanofi-Aventis, France) plus one capsule of placebo (900 mg arm), or two capsules with
51|300 mg rifampin (1,200-mg arm).
52|The study medications were taken together once daily in the morning 7 days per week with a glass
53|of water. In the case of gastrointestinal adverse effects, patients were allowed to take the pills with a light
54|meal.

11|Subsequently, a noncompartmental analysis with WinNonLin (version 6.3) software (Pharsight Corp.,
12|Mountain View, CA, USA) was performed to compute the values of the pharmacokinetic parameters for
13|rifampin, as described previously (11).
14|Safety and tolerability. Physical examination, testing of vital signs (including systolic and diastolic
15|blood pressure and heart rate), assessment of weight, biochemistry testing (AST, ALT, -glutamyl
16|transpeptidase, alkaline phosphatase, and creatinine), and hematology testing (hemoglobin, hematocrit,
17|red cell count, platelet count, total white cell count with differential) took place at screening and after
18|1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 weeks of treatment. In addition, at these visits the safety history was assessed
19|and concomitant medication was registered. Determination of fasting blood glucose levels was per-
20|formed only at screening.
21|Investigators reviewed each adverse event and assessed its relationship to drug treatment as
22|unrelated, possibly related, or related according to predefined definitions.
23|The severity of adverse events, including laboratory abnormalities, was classified following the U.S.
24|National Institutes of Health Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE; version 4.0) (25)
25|and reviewed by a data safety monitoring board.
26|Microbiological assessments. Spot sputum samples were collected for Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) staining
27|and direct microscopy before enrollment. For confirmation of the diagnosis, isolates from screening
28|cultures were identified as members of the M. tuberculosis complex using an AccuProbe assay (Gen-
29|Probe, San Diego, CA, USA) or a BD MGIT TBc identification test (BD Diagnostics, Sparks, MD, USA). These
30|screening isolates were also tested for susceptibility to streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol
31|by a commercial broth macrodilution test for the mycobacterial growth indicator tube (MGIT) platform
32|(SIRE; BD Bioscience, Erembodegem, Belgium) or a GenoType MTBDRplus assay (Hain Lifescience GmbH,
33|Nehren, Germany).
34|Pooled overnight (16 h) sputum samples were collected at the baseline and at days 2, 4, 7, 14, 21,
35|28, 35, 42, 49, and 56. All samples were processed for culture in the MGIT automated liquid culture
36|system as well as for culture on solid Lowenstein-Jensen medium (LJ); the latter was incubated for 8
37|weeks at 37°C. Pooled overnight sputum samples were also processed for counting of the colonies in
38|serial sputum samples; samples were diluted and plated in quadruplicate on selective Middlebrook 7H11
39|plates. The numbers of CFU per milliliter of sputum were calculated after a minimum of 21 days of
40|incubation at 37°C. In addition, the time to positivity (TTP) of the MGIT liquid culture was determined for
41|these samples to assess the change in TTP over time.
42|The study endpoints were defined as the time to culture conversion on LJ and in MGIT and the
43|proportion of patients that achieved culture conversion after 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 weeks, in addition to the
44|change in TTP in MGIT and the number of log CFU on Middlebrook 7H11 plates over time.
45|All sputum samples for microbiology were processed in the research microbiological laboratory of
46|KCMC. Procedures were performed according to the REMoxTB laboratory and quality manuals (26).
47|Statistical analysis. On the basis of experience obtained during a pharmacokinetic study of anti-TB
48|drugs in Botswana (27), it was estimated that 20 patients per arm would be needed to detect an increase
49|in total rifampin exposure in plasma of at least 35%, defined from the area under the concentration-
50|versus-time curve up to 24 h after the dose (AUC0-24), after an increase in the rifampin dose from 600
51|to 900 mg and from 900 to 1,200 mg (one-sided type I error, 0.05; 80% power; between-arm t test). To
52|obtain a more thorough insight into the safety and tolerability of higher than standard doses of rifampin,
53|the total number of patients per study arm was targeted at 50.
54|Pharmacokinetic parameters were presented descriptively and were log transformed before further
55|statistical analysis. Between-group differences in pharmacokinetic parameters were tested by one-way
56|analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis test for the time to the maximum plasma concentra-
57|tion (Tmax). Univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed for each of the arms
58|separately to assess the effects of gender, age, and body weight on the AUC0-24 and the maximum
59|plasma concentration (Cmax) of rifampin.
60|Safety was expressed as the incidence of adverse events by severity and relatedness, according to the
61|CTCAE criteria (25). The number of patients experiencing each event classified by system organ class
62|(SOC) was further specified for grade 3 adverse events.
63|The time to culture conversion between arms was compared using Cox proportional hazards
64|regression and by plotting Kaplan-Meier survival estimates. Cox proportional hazards regression was also
65|used to evaluate the effect of the actual rifampin dose received (in milligrams per kilogram) and the
66|rifampin exposures achieved (AUC0-24 and Cmax). The effect of exposure was evaluated by dichotomizing
67|each continuous parameter and by entering total and peak exposures as continuous variables. The
68|AUC0-24 or Cmax values of rifampin, isoniazid, or pyrazinamide were compared between those with and
69|those without grade 3 to 5 adverse events using an independent-groups t test.
